paras: The lynching of William Epperson took place on August 13, 1881, near Abbeville in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, when a crowd took him from the parish jail and hanged him. Epperson, a Black man, had been arrested that morning on the accusation that he murdered the wife and daughter of Pine Henderson, a Black resident of the parish. The local paper and the Baton Rouge press described the crowd as made up of both white and Black men and presented the hanging as deserved punishment.

On the night of Friday, August 12, Henderson, described by the Meridional as 'a worthy colored man,' left his wife and his daughter of about fourteen at home about two miles from Abbeville while he attended church in town. According to the Meridional, Epperson had been at the same church, 'more or less under the influence of liquor,' and left early cursing 'the whole people, white and black.' When Henderson returned he found his wife killed with an axe and her body mutilated, and the daughter was later found dead in a nearby wood with her head crushed. The papers stated that the daughter had been raped.

Henderson told the sheriff he suspected Epperson, and Sheriff G. B. Shaw and deputy George E. Lyons arrested him in bed at his house, his clothes stained with blood. He was lodged in the parish jail at Abbeville by about seven in the morning, where, the Meridional said, he confessed.

At about noon, by the local account, a crowd of 'the most worthy citizens' of the parish took him from the jail 'despite the powerless resistance of the officers.' The Louisiana Capitolian gave a fuller version: around 11 o'clock two or three hundred men, 'white and black,' brought a blacksmith with tools to break the doors, entered as the jailer was leaving, unshackled the prisoner and drove him by wagon to the place of the first murder, where a scaffold had been built. There, according to that paper, he confessed and, asked whether the crowd was right to hang him, answered that he thought so. The Donaldsonville Chief, summarizing the Meridional, said instead that the crowd 'hanged him to the nearest tree.'
No report of an inquest, of arrests of members of the crowd, or of any official action appears in the coverage found.

The Meridional of Abbeville reported the case on August 20 in both its English and French columns and openly defended the lynching, writing that 'no written law, no ordinary process of law' could reach such a crime and that 'a community has right, undeniable right to act.' Its French column had already said of the jailed man that 'il ne doit pas y rester longtemps.' The St. Landry Democrat of Opelousas reprinted the Meridional's English article in full on August 27.

The Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge ran the story on August 20 under the headline 'A Three-Fold Crime. Which is Summarily Punished with Instant Death, by an Outraged Population,' calling the accused 'Farrington' and describing the murders at length. On September 3 the Donaldsonville Chief paired the case with a shooting in Pointe Coupee Parish under 'Atrocious Crimes,' calling Epperson 'a drunken, quarrelsome Negro' and 'the black-hearted murderer' who 'acknowledged the justice of his punishment.' Every account stressed the mixed racial makeup of the crowd and the standing of the Henderson family, and none questioned the accused's guilt or the crowd's action.

The accounts differ on the accused's name, which the local paper gives as William Epperson and the Capitolian as William Farrington. They also differ on the hour, about 11 o'clock in the Capitolian and noon in the Meridional, and on the place of hanging, a scaffold at the murder scene in the Capitolian and 'the nearest tree' in the Chief.

framing.detail: Headlined 'A Three-Fold Crime. Which is Summarily Punished with Instant Death, by an Outraged Population', with a lurid account of the murders.
The local paper said honorable men were 'driven to sad necessities' and that a community had an 'undeniable right to act'; the French edition said he should not stay long in prison.
Called him 'the black-hearted murderer' who 'acknowledged the justice of his punishment'.

Taken from the parish jail at Abbeville; per the Capitolian hanged on a scaffold at the place of the first murder, the Henderson house about two miles from Abbeville (A1, A3); per the Donaldsonville Chief hanged 'to the nearest tree' (A6).
William Epperson (A2, A3, A6), called William Farrington by the Capitolian (A1); described as a 'negro' (A1, A6).
Accused of murdering with an axe the wife of Pine Henderson, a Black resident, and of raping and killing their daughter of about fourteen.
A crowd described as 'white and black' (A1), 'white and colored' (A6) and as 'the most worthy citizens of our Parish' (A3).
